name: Window of the World
label: Window of the World
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/236402460: large area 'Window of the World' (1366 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Theme park with miniature world landmarks and an Eiffel Tower replica.

text.description:
Window of the World is a theme park in Shenzhen where about 130 world landmarks have been rebuilt as scale models, so you can photograph several continents in one afternoon. The centrepiece is the Global Square, with a one-third-size Eiffel Tower standing 108 metres tall. Other replicas include Angkor Wat, Christ the Redeemer, the pyramids of Giza, the Sydney Opera House and the Taj Mahal. There is also a Manhattan skyline and a version of Mount Fuji. The park began construction in 1991 and opened on 18 June 1994. It is now a national 5A-level tourist attraction and gets more than 3.25 million visitors a year.

It photographs well because the landmarks are bold, familiar shapes, often set against open sky or water, so they read clearly even on a small phone screen. The park is big, about 1.4 km across, so wander a little and look for clean angles rather than shooting the first thing you see. Keep people out of the edges of the frame if you want the model to look like the real thing, or put a friend in the foreground for a playful sense of scale. Stand back far enough to fit tall structures like the tower without tilting the phone steeply, which makes the sides lean inward.
text.geographic_location: Window of the World is a large theme park in Shenzhen, China. The subject sits inside the park grounds.
text.directions_text: Start from central Shenzhen. The park has its own Shenzhen Metro station, Window of the World. Walk west from there to reach the subject. Check the official site before you go for entrances and the park layout. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most landmark shots. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the tall Eiffel Tower replica or for wide scenes, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as carvings and rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (plaza directly in front of the tower, facing it). The full Eiffel Tower replica framed from the open plaza in front of it, with warm light on the tower's stonework at golden hour. Shoot facing west so the models fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the tower's vertical line against a gridline so it stays straight. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) from a low position if you want the full height, and leave some sky above. For a people shot, place your friend a few steps in front of the model and use portrait mode so the replica stays recognisable in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the landmark to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright so the sky and stonework keep their detail. Live Photos are good for water features and moving crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light and less glare off pale stonework. If the park is open in the evening, night mode can work on lit structures; check the official site for times.

text.access_note: This is a themed attraction that is likely to need an entry ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ping An Finance Centre
label: Ping An Finance Centre
camera_source: Commons cluster (5 photos), weak. Moved 47 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 280 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/535860513: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ping An Finance Center' (108 m across).
notes: Supertall skyscraper that dominates the Futian skyline.

text.description: Ping An Finance Centre is the tallest building in Shenzhen. It has 115 storeys, stands 599.1 metres high and was completed in 2017. The tower is slim, about ten times taller than it is wide, and its stainless-steel facade reflects the sky. It was designed by the American firm Kohn Pedersen Fox and is the headquarters of Ping An Insurance. A public observation deck called Free Sky sits on floor 116. That distance suits a phone well. Tilt the phone upwards and the sides of the tower will lean inwards, so try to keep the phone as upright as you can and leave some space around the top of the building. Include a foreground such as a tree, a lamp post or a pedestrian crossing to give a sense of size. If you want a cleaner, more graphic picture, step back until the tower sits centrally and use the gridlines to keep the edges straight. A second, smaller tower stands beside it as part of the same complex, and it can add depth if it falls into your frame.
text.geographic_location: In the Futian district, in Shenzhen's Central Business District. It is the tallest of the towers around it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Futian Central Business District. Walk east towards the tower and you will see it rising above the surrounding buildings. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower from where you stand. The default lens (1x) works for the upper half or for a tighter, more graphic crop. Telephoto (2x-5x) is good for the pointed top and the facade pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Deng Xiaoping Statue Square (Lianhuashan Park summit) (summit terrace; left side of the main upper terrace, shooting slightly down at the tower). The tower rises on the right of a wide Futian CBD panorama, with the Civic Center and other towers in the middle ground. About 5 minutes on foot from the tower base. Pick a spot with a clear sightline between the nearer buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn gridlines on and line the tower up with a vertical line. Hold the phone as upright as you can so the sides do not lean in too much. Leave a little sky above the top. Add a foreground like trees or a street feature for scale. Try a portrait-orientation shot first, then a wider landscape version that includes the neighbouring towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the metal. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows against a wall or railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk, when the facade can pick up warm light and the building lights come on. Blue hour gives a good balance between sky and lit windows.

text.access_note: The tower can be photographed from the surrounding public streets. If you plan to visit the Free Sky observation deck, check the official site before you go.

name: Splendid China Folk Village
label: Splendid China
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/236402467: large area 'Splendid China Folk Village' (1609 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Splendid China Folk Village is a theme park beside Shenzhen Bay. It has two parts: a miniature park and a folk culture village. More than 100 major sights from across China have been rebuilt as models and laid out roughly according to the map of China. Most are at about 1:15 scale. The Great Wall, the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace, the Three Gorges Dam, the Potala Palace and the Terracotta Army are among them. The whole park covers about 30 hectares, so it is large, and cars and trains run between areas.

For a phone photographer the appeal is the play of scale. Close up, a model temple or wall section can look like the real thing, and a person standing beside it shows the trick at once. The park is big, so choose one or two models you like rather than trying to cover everything. Walk up to a model, crouch so your phone is near its base, and shoot level with it. Keep the background simple so the model looks full-size. For a wider view, step back and include the paths and planting around it. Save a few frames for the shows and the folk village if they are running, as they add people and colour. Photo rules can vary inside parks like this, so follow any signs.
text.geographic_location: In Shenzhen's Overseas Chinese Town (OCT) tourist area, beside Shenzhen Bay, within the Shenzhen Special Economic Zone.
text.directions_text: No metro station is listed for this spot, so head for the Overseas Chinese Town (OCT) area by Shenzhen Bay. If you are coming from the Luohu side of the city, the journey from Luohu Station on Line 1 of the Shenzhen Metro takes about 35-40 minutes by train. Bus 101 and mini-bus 23 are also given as examples, at about 30 minutes from Luohu. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for single models. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a whole group of models with the sky behind. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out roof details and to flatten the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 风雨桥 (Wind and Rain Bridge) (lakeside approach, facing the Cui Lake performance area). The covered wooden bridge in the foreground, with the lit lake and performance area behind it, especially during the evening show. Then walk on to other models you like.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch so the phone is level with the base of a model, and keep other visitors and signs out of the frame so the scale looks real. Turn on gridlines to keep rooflines and walls straight. For a wider view, step back and use 0.5x, but keep the edges clear of bins and railings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the model to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Portrait mode can blur the background behind a close model, but check that the edges look clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the park is open and the light is softer, such as morning or late afternoon, rather than the harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: Check opening and entry details before you go.

name: Huaqiangbei
label: Huaqiangbei
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '华强北路' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).

text.description: Huaqiangbei is Shenzhen's electronics district, and it photographs like a big-city street rather than a sight. It is a subdistrict of Futian and has one of the largest electronics markets in the world. In 2020 it had about 38,000 businesses, and that density shows in the stacked shopfronts, glowing signs and tall commercial towers on both sides of the street. The pedestrian stretch of Huaqiang North Road is the best place to catch it. The tree-lined streets have wide footpaths, so you can stop and frame a shot without blocking the way. The district runs about a kilometre north from Shennan Road at SEG Plaza, with Huaqiang Road at its centre. Traffic, people and shop lights fill the frame, and the towers rise above them. Late afternoon into early evening is a good time, when the street is at its busiest and the lights start to come on. Keep your phone at chest height and wait for a gap in the crowd, or include the crowd on purpose to show how lively it is. Watch your bag and phone in busy spots.
text.geographic_location: Huaqiangbei is in Futian district, central Shenzhen. It runs north from Shennan Road at SEG Plaza, with Huaqiang Road as its busy pedestrian spine.
text.directions_text: Go to Huaqiang North Road. Huaqiang North station (Line 2 and Line 7) of the Shenzhen Metro is in the area. The centre of the district lies about 570 m to the east, a short walk from there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural street view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to fit in the tall towers and the whole width of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on 华强北路 (Huaqiang North Road), on the pedestrian stretch on the west side of Qunxing Plaza. Face along the street so you see the commercial towers, traffic and shopfront lights on both sides. The centre of the district is to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the street up with the centre of the frame, so the buildings lead the eye down it. Keep the phone level so the towers don't lean. Include a few people for scale and wait for a gap if you want the street clearer. A telephoto/zoom lens (2x-5x) can pick out a single glowing sign or a crowded shopfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the street to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights don't wash out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or railing, or tuck your elbows in, to stay steady. Live Photos can catch the movement of traffic and people.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: 5 PM to 7 PM, when the towers, traffic and shop lights are all busiest. The street is also lively after dark.

text.access_note: The pedestrian street is open public space, but individual shops and malls have their own rules, so check before photographing inside and look out for posted signs.
claims_not_in_sources: A level phone and gridlines help keep tall buildings from leaning.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit tall towers and a wide street into one frame.
Night mode works better when the phone is braced against something steady.
Busy pavements mean you may need to wait for a gap in the crowd.
Take care of your bag and phone in crowded areas.
The pedestrian stretch is a public street that does not need a ticket.

name: Shenzhen Stock Exchange
label: Stock Exchange
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Shenzhen Stock Exchange' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/923157986: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Shenzhen Stock Exchange' (216 m across).
notes: Building with a lifted base and a floating look.

text.description:
The Shenzhen Stock Exchange is a tall, boxy tower on Shennan Boulevard in Futian. Its wide, raised podium looks as if it is floating above the ground, and that is what draws the eye. It is a good place for a phone photo because the shape is so unusual. The building is 245.8 metres tall with 49 floors, and it was built between 2008 and 2013. It was designed by the Office for Metropolitan Architecture, Rem Koolhaas's firm. The exchange itself was founded on 1 December 1990.

The classic view is from the front plaza, looking at the main facade. A bull sculpture sits in the foreground, which gives you a ready-made subject for the lower part of the frame. Other Futian towers rise behind the building, so the photo says 'Shenzhen business district' straight away. Daytime suits the architectural detail. Early evening is good for the building lit against the twilight.

Stay on the public pavement and plaza. Security at financial buildings may turn people away from the lobby, so don't plan any photos inside. If you want a wider skyline picture with the exchange as a small part of it, Lianhuashan Park is a distant alternative. There the exchange is on the left and Ping An Finance Centre on the right, and a zoom lens helps.
text.geographic_location: In Futian District, Shenzhen, on Shennan Boulevard, among the towers of Futian's central business area.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so a taxi or walking from central Futian is the practical way to get there. Ask for the Shenzhen Stock Exchange on Shennan Boulevard, Futian District. The subject on the map marks the middle of the building's outline, not the viewpoint. Get out at the front of the building, where the plaza and the bull sculpture are, and walk to the plaza. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower, the podium and the bull sculpture into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the facade. Try telephoto (2x-5x) for detail on the facade and the surrounding towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The middle of the building's outline on the map is the subject, so you cannot frame the facade from there. Walk to the public front plaza, near the bull sculpture, and step back to face the main facade. From there you see the raised podium and facade, framed by the bull sculpture and the Futian towers behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the bull sculpture low in the frame as a foreground anchor and let the podium and tower fill the rest. Turn on gridlines and keep the phone as level as you can, so the vertical lines stay straight. If the tower will not fit, step back or use the ultra-wide (0.5x) rather than tilting the phone steeply upwards. For a different view, Lianhuashan Park gives a distant skyline with the exchange on the left; use zoom there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the building keeps its detail. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing for sharper lit-up shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime for architectural detail, and early evening for the building lit against twilight.

text.access_note: The plaza and pavement outside are public and photography there is generally allowed, but security may turn people away from the lobby, so check the official site before you go if you want to enter.

name: Lianhuashan Park
label: Lianhuashan Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '风筝广场' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '风筝广场' (way/617152039): middle (403 m across).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Hilltop park with the Deng Xiaoping statue and city views.

text.description:
Lianhuashan Park (Lotus Hill Park) is a large hill park at the northern end of Futian's Central Business District, opened in 1997 and covering about 150 hectares. For photographs, the appeal is the contrast between open green slopes and the towers of the city behind them. The best-known landmark is the 6-metre bronze statue of Deng Xiaoping on the hilltop. It shows him walking briskly, and it was unveiled in November 2000. The statue sits at the head of a long line of sight running south through Futian, which is why the city seems to fan out below the park.

For an easy, relaxed shot, start at the kite square (风筝广场) on the way up. Its large lawn slopes gently, so friends or family can stand on the grass while the skyline fills the background. If you have the energy for the summit, 山顶广场 has the wide view over the business district, with the statue in the foreground. The lake, 莲花湖, is a quieter place for reflections of the lakeside trees.

The park is big and hilly, so wear comfortable shoes. Take your photos early on busy days, because the summit fills up later in the afternoon. Haze can soften the skyline, so a clear day makes a real difference.
text.geographic_location: Lianhuashan Park is in Futian District, Shenzhen, at the northern end of the Futian Central Business District. The kite square lies on the slope on the way up from the South Gate.
text.directions_text: The park is within walking distance of Children's Palace Station on the Shenzhen Metro. From the South Gate, follow the path uphill and the kite square is an easy stop on the way up. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the lawn and skyline together. Switch to 2x or 3x telephoto, if your phone has it, for portraits so the towers look closer behind your subject. The ultra-wide (0.5x) suits the sweep of the open lawn.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 风筝广场 (gentle slope of the large lawn, with the skyline behind). Portrait-style shots of people on the open lawn with the city skyline in the background. Face towards the city with your subject on the grass and the skyline behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place your subject a little below the horizon line so the towers rise behind them rather than out of their head. Turn on the gridlines to keep the skyline level. For a wide city panorama with the statue in front, walk up to 山顶广场 instead. For reflections, try the lake, 莲花湖.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Use portrait mode for people on the lawn, and tap on their face to set focus. Then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. On hazy days, a little less brightness keeps the skyline from looking flat.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go earlier in the day if you can, as the summit gets crowded after about 16:00. Pick a clear day, since haze often reduces skyline visibility.

text.access_note: This is a public park, but opening hours can vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Shenzhen Museum
label: Shenzhen Museum
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3829834370: the OpenStreetMap point 'Shenzhen Museum History and Culture Museum'.
notes: City history museum facing the Civic Center.

text.description:
Shenzhen Museum is a public municipal museum, and this spot is its History and Folk Culture branch in the Civic Center, sometimes called the Jintian Road branch. The museum as a whole is run across four sites, so it is worth knowing you are at the one that tells the story of Shenzhen and its people. The collection holds more than 20,000 historical and cultural relics, most of them found within the city itself. The original museum was set up in 1981 and only formally opened in 1988. That earlier building is now the Shenzhen Museum of Ancient Art, on Tongxin Road.

For photographs, the main appeal is the building in its Civic Center setting. It makes a clear, calm subject that sits well in a straight-on frame, and it gives you a good sense of how the modern city is laid out. Plan on fitting the whole structure in with the ultra-wide lens rather than backing away. Keep your phone level, switch on the gridlines and line the building up with them, so the verticals stay straight. A second shot with a person walking past can give a good sense of scale. Inside, photography rules can differ from room to room, so follow any signs.
text.geographic_location: In Shenzhen's Civic Center area. It is the museum's History and Folk Culture branch, also called the Jintian Road branch.
text.directions_text: No Metro station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for the Civic Center and use the phone icon on the map. Once you reach it, the building is about 18 m to the south-east, roughly 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) because you are standing very close to the building. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view of the entrance or one section. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for details such as signs or the roof line.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Face that way and keep the building in the middle of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so it does not lean. Keep the phone upright and level. Try one wide shot that includes the open space in front for scale, then one tighter shot at 1x or 2x of the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps some detail. Live Photos can help if people are crossing the frame, because you can pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the front of the building. Early in the day is also likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: This is a public museum, so access and entry arrangements may apply; check the official site before you go.

name: Shenzhen Convention and Exhibition Center
label: Convention Center
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Shenzhen Convention and Exhibition Center' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/146862823: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Shenzhen Convention & Exhibition Center' (626 m across).
notes: Huge glass-and-steel exhibition hall in Futian.

text.description: The Shenzhen Convention and Exhibition Center is a huge public building in Futian Central Business District, and its sheer size is what you notice first. It covers 280,000 square metres, is about 540 metres long and 282 metres wide, and stands 60 metres tall. It was completed in 2004 and was designed by the German firm Gerkan, Marg and Partners. From outside, the wave-shaped exterior is the main subject, and the Futian high-rises rise behind it, so a single frame can show the low, long building against the towers. A visitor review suggests you can walk all the way round the outdoor grounds, so you can try several angles instead of settling for the first one. The building is too wide to fit in one shot from close by, so step back and use the ultra-wide lens, or move along the grounds and take two or three frames of different sections. Look for the curved lines of the roof and facade, which make a good pattern in close-up. If you want a street-level view of the facade, Binhe Boulevard runs past the centre and is a useful second spot. Exhibitions are held here regularly, so the grounds may be busier on event days. The phone icon on the map sits at the centre of the building's mapped outline, so treat it as a reference for the building rather than a place to shoot from. Use the outdoor grounds around the building for your exterior shots.
text.geographic_location: In Futian Central Business District, Shenzhen. It is a large exhibition and conference building with the Futian high-rises around and beyond it.
text.directions_text: Convention and Exhibition Center Station, on Shenzhen Metro lines 1 and 4, serves the building and its surroundings. From the station, walk to the outdoor grounds around the building and use the stand-here marker as a reference for the building's centre. A taxi to the Convention and Exhibition Center also works if you prefer. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get the long, wave-shaped building into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out roof curves and the towers behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk to the outdoor grounds around it and frame the exterior from there, where the wave-shaped facade and the Futian high-rises beyond come into view. Walk round the grounds to find the angle you like best, and try Binhe Boulevard for a street-level view of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the building's long edges so the horizontals stay level. Keep the towers behind it in the top part of the frame to show where you are. Back away as far as the grounds allow before using the ultra-wide lens, and keep the building away from the very edges of the frame, where ultra-wide shots stretch things. If you prefer a street-level shot, Binhe Boulevard is the alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. Panorama mode is worth trying along the grounds, but hold the phone steady and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to a big facade than harsh midday sun, and daylight shows the Futian towers behind it clearly.

text.access_note: The outdoor grounds are described as walkable all the way round, but access inside depends on events, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is generally kinder to a large facade than harsh midday sun.
The grounds may be busier on days when an exhibition or conference is on.
Ultra-wide shots can stretch objects near the edges of the frame.

name: Shenzhen Museum of Contemporary Art and Urban Planning
label: MOCAUP
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '市民广场' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '市民广场' (way/183106115): edge nearest the subject (693 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/456331569: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Museum of Contemporary Art & Planning Exhibition (MOCAPE)' (214 m across).
notes: Modern twin museum building by Coop Himmelb(l)au.

text.description: This is a big, modern museum in Futian District, and it photographs well because of its shape: a sweeping curved metal facade that picks up the sky and the colours of the city. It was designed by the architects Coop Himmelb(l)au and opened in 2016. The site covers roughly 29,700 square metres, with about 88,000 square metres of floor space inside. Its permanent exhibitions cover Shenzhen's urban planning, its landmarks and its history of reform and opening up. The best outdoor photo is taken from the central axis of the square in front, beside the reflecting pool. Get low and hold the phone just above the water's edge to make the reflection stronger. The pool and square are the quieter, simpler option. If you go inside, the guides single out the mirror-polished cloud sculpture, the steel dome and the curving spiral staircase, where light and shadow layer nicely. Indoor visits need a booking, so reserve through the museum's WeChat official account before you go. Drone flying nearby is unlikely to be allowed, so plan your pictures for the ground.
text.geographic_location: In Futian District, Shenzhen, at the museum and the square called 市民广场 in front of it.
text.directions_text: Head for Futian District and look for the Shenzhen Museum of Contemporary Art and Urban Planning, which is served by Shenzhen Metro (Civic Center and Children's Palace stations). Make your way to the square in front of the museum. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole curved facade and its reflection in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the metal surface and the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 市民广场 (central axis in front of the museum, by the reflecting pool). A wide frontal view of the museum's curved metal facade, with the building and sky reflected in the water in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch and hold the phone low over the pool so the reflection fills the lower half of the picture. Turn on the gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower line, with the facade centred above it. If you go indoors (booking needed), try looking up at the cloud sculpture and dome, or down the spiral staircase.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright metal and sky don't wash out. Turn on the gridlines to keep the building straight. Wait for a gap in any ripples before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a calm day, when the water is still and the reflection is clearest. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the metal.

text.access_note: The outdoor square and pool are open public space, but entering the museum needs a reservation and may involve ID, and it is reportedly closed on Mondays, so reserve through the museum's WeChat official account before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Still, windless water gives the clearest reflection in the pool.
Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the metal facade.
A phone held low over the water's edge strengthens the reflection.

name: Shenzhen Civic Center
label: Civic Center
camera_source: Commons cluster (29 photos). Moved 84 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 340 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/10837975: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Civic Center' (521 m across).
notes: Government building with a giant wave-like roof.

text.description:
Shenzhen Civic Center is the city's government building, and its big sweeping roof is what makes it such a good photo subject. The roof curves like a pair of wings. The design is based on a traditional Southern Chinese roof form and nods to Shenzhen's nickname, the "Eagle City". The roof spans 486 metres, and the building stands 84.7 metres tall. That makes it a long, low-looking shape, which suits a wide phone frame.

The long roof truss went up in 1998, but the roof was not clad until 2004. The building sits on a central axis that runs about 2 km from Lianhua Mountain in the north, through the Civic Center, to the Exhibition Center in the south. It is also used as a popular viewing point for celebrations and for drone and LED light shows.

Use the roof's long line as the main feature of the picture, and keep the horizon level using the gridlines. Wait for a few walkers to cross the foreground if you want a sense of scale. The roof is very wide, so decide first whether you want the whole sweep or just one part of it.
text.geographic_location: In the Futian Central Business District of Shenzhen, on the city's central axis between Lianhua Mountain to the north and the Exhibition Center to the south.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Futian Central Business District and look for the Civic Center (市民中心). From there the Civic Center is to the south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole roof in. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched look, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a section of the roof or the towers beneath it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Civic Center Square (central axis, facing the main building from the front steps and lawn). The civic building head-on across the wide plaza, with the surrounding Futian towers behind it, and reflections on the ground on sunny days.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the roof up with a horizontal line so it does not slope. Keep the whole roof in view with a little space above it. For a different look, try panorama mode and hold the phone upright, moving slowly from one end of the roof to the other.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the roof does not turn into a silhouette. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone as steady as you can, resting your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives the clearest view of the roof's shape. Since you are facing south, the sun can be behind the building around midday, so early morning or late afternoon may suit you better. If a light show is on, evenings are worth trying.

text.access_note: The area around the building is open to walk through, but the building holds government offices and a museum, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Shenzhen Library
label: Shenzhen Library
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '莲花山公园' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '莲花山公园' (way/41281446): edge nearest the subject (2250 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/146867406: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Shenzhen Library' (159 m across).
notes: Modern library next to the Concert Hall.

text.description:
Shenzhen Library is the city's main public library, and it forms one half of a matching pair with the neighbouring concert hall. Both buildings sit in Futian, part of the Shenzhen Cultural Center, with the tall towers of the Futian business district rising behind them. The best way to photograph them is from a distance. From up there you can fit the whole cluster into one frame, with the skyline as a backdrop. In the evening the buildings are lit, which makes the picture much more striking.

A few facts help explain what you are looking at. The main library has a floor area of about 49,600 square metres on a plot of roughly 29,600 square metres, so it is a very large building. Its predecessor opened in 1986 in the north-west area of Lychee Park, and building work had started in 1983.

For your phone, think of this as a view rather than a close-up. Stay at the summit, use the zoom to pick out the two buildings, and keep the skyline behind them. Wait for the lights to come on if you can. If the summit is crowded, try another angle later: the Citizen Center square gives a wide view along the central axis, and the Book City rooftop looks over Fuzhong 1st Road. Check the official site before you go for entry and access to either.
text.geographic_location: The library is in Futian District, in the centre of Shenzhen, as part of the Shenzhen Cultural Center. It stands right beside 莲花山公园 (Lianhua Mountain Park).
text.directions_text: Head for the Futian area in central Shenzhen and aim for 莲花山公园 (Lianhua Mountain Park), which is next to the library. The way down is by the park paths, so allow more time. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the library and concert hall from the summit. The default lens (1x) works for a wider view that includes the skyline and the park around you. Ultra-wide (0.5x) tends to make the buildings look very small from this distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 莲花山公园 (summit of the hill, looking back down at the library and concert hall). A distant panoramic view of the twin library and concert hall buildings, lit up in the evening, with the Futian CBD skyline behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the two buildings on the lower third, so the skyline fills the space above. Zoom in until they fill the width of the frame. If you want a different angle, the Citizen Center square gives a wide view along the central axis, with the library and concert hall at the side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the buildings to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights do not turn into white patches. After dark, use night mode and lean your elbows on a wall or railing to keep steady. Hold still until the shot finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, once the buildings are lit. Dusk gives you both the glow of the lights and some colour left in the sky.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for the park's entry arrangements; the same applies to the Citizen Center light-show viewing area and the Book City rooftop.

name: KK100
label: KK100
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '荔枝公园' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '荔枝公园' (way/178426795): edge nearest the subject (1062 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/164033632: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kingkey 100' (82 m across).

text.description:
KK100 is a 100-storey tower, 442 m tall, and the second tallest building in Shenzhen. It is also one of China's slimmest, about 9.5 times taller than it is wide, so it reads as a clean, thin line against the sky. That shape suits a phone held upright. From the lakeside in 荔枝公园 (Lizhi Park), the tower rises above the water and the lychee trees, with the Luohu skyline around it. The park, the water and the trees give you a ground-level frame that is easy to compose.

The tower stands on Shennan East Road in Caiwuwei, an area often called Shenzhen's financial district. Offices fill most of the floors. A hotel takes the upper levels, and the top four floors hold a garden and restaurants. The KK Mall sits next to it, and a water fountain stands in front of the building.

For your photo, stand by the lake and let the water fill the bottom of the frame, with the tower rising from the trees behind. If you want a second angle, walk over to the base of the tower. From close range you can capture its full height with the fountain in the foreground. Keep the tower upright and centred, and check that the lines of the building are not leaning. The gridlines in your camera app make this easy.
text.geographic_location: KK100 is in Shenzhen's Luohu District, in the Caiwuwei area on Shennan East Road. It stands just east of Lizhi Park, about a kilometre north of the border with Hong Kong.
text.directions_text: Take the metro to Grand Theater station and walk to 荔枝公园 (Lizhi Park). From there the tower is about 226 m to the east, a short walk of a few minutes, if you want the close-up view with the fountain. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the lakeside so the tower, water and trees all fit. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only when you are close to the base and need the whole height; keep the phone level to limit the leaning effect. Use the telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 荔枝公园 (lakeside, looking toward the tower across the water). KK100 rising above the lake and lychee trees of the park, with the Luohu skyline around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on the gridlines. Put the tower on one of the vertical lines and keep a strip of water at the bottom of the frame. Frame the trees along the edges so they lead the eye up. If you also visit the base of the tower, use the fountain as your foreground and tilt the phone up gently.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the glass keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or your body against a post to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and calmer water. Dusk can also work well if the tower is lit.

text.access_note: 荔枝公园 is a public park, but check the official site before you go for any rules on the park, and for the tower's observation deck, which may be ticketed.
claims_not_in_sources: Calm water in the lake can give a reflection of the tower.
Morning and late afternoon usually give softer light.
The tower may be lit at dusk.
Trees at the lakeside may block the lower part of the tower from some spots.
Resting your elbows on a railing helps keep a phone steady in night mode.

name: Shun Hing Square
label: Shun Hing Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '深南东路' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '深南东路' (way/272771512): point nearest the subject (899 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/64601041: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Shun Hing Square' (87 m across).
notes: Landmark 1990s tower, also called Diwang Building.

text.description:
Shun Hing Square, also called Di Wang Tower or Diwang Building, is a slender steel skyscraper that stands out in central Shenzhen. It is 384 metres tall and has 69 floors. When it was finished in 1996 it was the tallest building in China, a title it held only until CITIC Plaza in Guangzhou opened the following year. It is still described as the tallest all-steel building in China. It went up at a pace of four floors in nine days, and its nickname comes from the record price paid for the land it stands on.

It photographs well because it is tall, narrow and simple in outline, so it reads clearly even among neighbouring towers. The road and the surrounding buildings lead the eye towards the tower, so the street does a lot of the composing for you. The tower is some distance away from here, so think of it as a picture of the skyline with the tower as the main subject, not a close-up of the building.

If you want other views, the base of the tower gives a steep upward shot with other office blocks in the frame. Lizhi Park gives a calmer, more distant view with the tower rising above the trees. Take care at the roadside and keep clear of traffic and the pavement flow while you frame your shot.
text.geographic_location: Shun Hing Square is in central Shenzhen, near the Kingkey 100 tower.
text.directions_text: To reach the tower itself, Grand Theater Station (Lines 1, 2 and 5, Exit D) is the station for reaching the tower and its observation deck. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer and fill more of the frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) if you want more of the avenue and surrounding towers. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is best saved for the base of the tower, where you can fit the whole height in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 深南东路 (stretch facing the tower, with the building framed down the avenue). The tower seen from the road side, with the wide avenue and surrounding towers leading the eye toward it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines so the avenue leads the eye to it. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean. Lizhi Park gives a more distant view with the tower above the trees, and the base of the tower gives a steep upward shot, if you would like an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the glass does not turn white. A quick burst of Live Photo can help catch a moment when traffic is clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. From this side the tower is to the west, so morning light should fall on the face you are looking at. At dusk or night, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.

text.access_note: The roadside is public pavement, but the 69th-floor observation deck and the building itself may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Shenzhen Grand Theater
label: Grand Theater
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Shenzhen Grand Theater' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/179274427: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Shenzhen Grand Theatre' (177 m across).

text.description:
Shenzhen Grand Theater is a large arts building in Luohu District, on Shennan East Road. It was one of the "Eight Major Cultural Facilities" the city built in its early years as a Special Economic Zone. Building began in 1984 and it opened in 1989, so it is a good reminder of how young Shenzhen is. The outside is glass curtain walling in a folded, cube-like design. Inside, the main hall has more than 1,600 seats, and the complex also holds a concert hall, exhibition space and an underground shopping street.

It photographs best in the evening. After dark the facade and gateway are lit in yellow and gold, and tall illuminated towers stand behind it, which gives your photo a sense of the city around it. In daylight the glass and angled shapes still make clean, graphic pictures, but the evening light show is the reason to come.

Walk to the open area in front of the entrance and face the building from there. The theatre is big, so you will need to step back to fit it in, or use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) if you cannot. Keep the phone level, using the gridlines, so the vertical lines do not lean. For a different view, some visitors suggest an elevated spot near the Grand Theater Station exits for a higher angle; check on your map app. If you go inside for a performance, photography is not allowed during the show.
text.geographic_location: In Luohu District, Shenzhen, at No. 5018 Shennan East Road. Grand Theater Station on Line 2 of the Shenzhen Metro serves the theatre.
text.directions_text: Take Line 2 of the Shenzhen Metro to Grand Theater Station, which is named after the theatre. Once you are out of the station, follow the signs and your map app to the theatre. When you are close, head for the open area in front of the entrance rather than the building itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade and gateway. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the whole building will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for details of the glass and the lights.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk to the open area in front of the entrance and face the building from there, stepping back until it fits. The photo then shows the facade and gateway, lit in yellow and gold after dark, with the lit towers behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with them so the verticals stay straight. Include the gateway in the foreground and let the lit towers sit behind as background. For a different angle, some visitors suggest an elevated spot near the Grand Theater Station exits for a higher view of the theatre and the Luohu skyline; check on your map app.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and hold the phone as still as you can, resting your elbows against your body or a wall. Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the gold lights do not blow out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: In the evening after dark, when the building and the towers behind it are lit. Daytime is fine for the glass and folded shapes.

text.access_note: The area in front of the theatre is a public space; performances inside need tickets and photography is not allowed during them, so check the official site before you go.

name: Shenzhen Special Zone Press Tower
label: Press Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '莲花山公园山顶广场' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '中国工商银行' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/925221216: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Shenzhen Special Zone Press Tower' (119 m across).
notes: Skyscraper with a distinctive open-frame top.

text.description:
The Shenzhen Special Zone Press Tower is an office skyscraper in Futian, completed in 1998. It has 47 floors above ground and 3 underground, and is listed at 260 m. The building has a curved glass curtain wall below its main roof. It stands on the north side of Shennan Avenue (6008 Shennan Boulevard), opposite the Tianan golf course, with the Lotus Hill park area behind it to the north.

It photographs well because it is tall, glassy and fairly slim, so you can make it a strong vertical shot or a clean modern backdrop for a travel photo. Expect the sides to lean inwards. That is normal for tall buildings, and it can look dramatic if you keep it deliberate and centred.

For a calmer, more even shot, step back along the pavement until you can use the default lens (1x) and still see the whole building. Use the gridlines to keep the edges roughly upright. Then try the telephoto lens for a close-up of the curved glass curtain wall. Watch out for traffic and signs at the bottom of the frame. For a wider skyline view over Futian, the summit plaza in Lotus Hill Park is worth a look, but check that the tower is actually in your frame from there.
text.geographic_location: In Futian District, Shenzhen, on the north side of Shennan Avenue, opposite the Tianan golf course. Lotus Hill Park lies to the north.
text.directions_text: The nearest stations are not listed, so start from the Futian area on Shennan Avenue and head for number 6008, on the north side of the road, opposite the Tianan golf course. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close, because the tower is very tall. Switch to the default lens (1x) once you have stepped back, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the curved glass curtain wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 莲花山公园山顶广场. A skyline view over the Futian core, with the tower somewhere among the surrounding high-rises; no source confirms it is framed from here. Point the phone up and to the north-west. If you want a wider skyline picture, the summit plaza in Lotus Hill Park is an alternative. It gives a view over the Futian high-rises, with the tower somewhere among them, so check that it is in frame before you rely on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright (portrait) and use the gridlines to keep the sides of the tower near vertical. Keep the phone level rather than tilting it too far, or step back to reduce the lean. Leave a little sky above the roofline so the top is not cropped. For a second shot, zoom in on the curved glass curtain wall alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glass to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building does not turn into a silhouette.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime in clear weather gives clean glass and a blue sky. Around dusk, the sky and the lit city can look good, and you can try night mode with the phone held steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The tower is an office building, so the surrounding pavements are the public place to take photos from. Check the official site before you go if you want to go inside, and do not rely on getting into the lobby or any upper floors.
claims_not_in_sources: Tall buildings photographed from close range with an ultra-wide lens show converging verticals (leaning sides).
Clear daytime weather gives clean views of glass facades.
Dusk and night photography of the lit city may suit this area.
The pavements around the tower are public, while the interior is an office building with likely restricted access.
Lotus Hill Park's summit plaza gives a wider view over Futian, but check on the day that the tower is in frame from there.
The Lotus Hill summit plaza is far from the stand-here point (tower 40 m to the north-west), so it is mentioned only as an alternative.
